states.source: KNBS — 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census Reports
states.reason: KNBS's 2019 KPHC publication does not publish average household size as a direct current-290-constituency table. County/sub-county values are not inherited, and lower administrative-unit household counts are not aggregated without an authoritative constituency crosswalk; the older KNBS constituency table predates the current 2012-01 constituency configuration. P28A re-audit (2026-09-16) independently re-verified this by downloading and text-extracting KNBS 2019 KPHC Volume II (Distribution of Population by Administrative Units, https://www.knbs.or.ke/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/2019-Kenya-population-and-Housing-Census-Volume-2-Distribution-of-Population-by-Administrative-Units.pdf) in full: its own List of Tables shows Table 2.4 (Distribution of Population by Sex, Number of Households, Land Area, Population Density and Sub Locations) is the finest administrative tier published -- there is no Table 2.x for constituencies. 'Constituency' and 'Ward' appear in Volume II exactly twice, both times as fields on the raw household enumeration questionnaire reproduced in the appendix, not as a published aggregate table -- a census questionnaire field recording constituency does not by itself constitute a published constituency statistic (see rules, above). The re-audit also confirmed KNBS administrative sub-counties (the finest county-nested tier that is aggregated, in Table 2.3) are not the same delineation as the 290 IEBC electoral constituencies and cannot substitute for them without a crosswalk KNBS has not published: e.g. Table 1.2 lists 5 KNBS sub-counties for Kwale County (Kinango, Lunga Lunga, Matuga, Msambweni, Samburu) against Kwale's 4 IEBC constituencies, and 11 KNBS sub-counties for Meru County against Meru's 9 IEBC constituencies. Separately, the re-audit downloaded and text-extracted the older, standalone 'Constituency Population by Sex, Number of Households, Area and Density' publication (https://www.knbs.or.ke/constituency-population-by-sex-number-of-households-area-and-density/, republished 2013) and confirmed it is 2009-census Volume 1B (Population Distribution by Political Units), whose own text states its tables 'are tabulated for the 210 constituencies and the 47 counties in Kenya' -- i.e. it is definitively the pre-2012-delimitation constituency configuration referenced above, not a current-290 table, and using it to derive household size (population / households) would require exactly the unavailable 210-to-290 crosswalk this closure already prohibits inventing. The re-audit also checked the KNBS Kenya National Data Archive (NADA) catalog entry for the 2019 KPHC (https://statistics.knbs.or.ke/nada/index.php/catalog/116); its public study metadata documents no constituency-level geographic identifier or downloadable constituency aggregate and describes geographic coverage only at 'The Whole Country' / household-and-individual microdata level, not a released constituency tabulation. No credible S0-S4 primary or secondary source, and no defensible S1 official-derived computation (an authoritative population figure and an authoritative household-count figure at the same current-290-constituency granularity), was found. As of this re-audit, IEBC has also publicly ruled out any constituency/ward boundary delimitation review before the 2027 general election -- the constitutional March 2024 deadline was missed, and a January 2025 High Court ruling (under appeal) invalidated the underlying 2019 census population figures for Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties specifically -- so the current 2012-01, 290-constituency boundary remains the operative geography with no imminent republication of constituency-level census tables or a fresh KNBS-IEBC crosswalk in prospect.
states.refresh_trigger: KNBS publishes a direct current-290 constituency household-size table (population and household counts both tabulated at current-constituency granularity), or an authoritative 2019 administrative-unit (or 2009-to-2012 delimitation) to 2012-01 constituency crosswalk that KNBS or IEBC has certified as exact and complete.

states.period_label: Research review as at 8 September 2026 · no enacted uniform national ward-fund programme
states.source: National Government Constituencies Development Fund Act, 2015 (as amended 2022/2023); County Wards (Equitable Development) Bill, 2024 (Kenya Parliament, not enacted); illustrative county-specific Ward Development Fund legislation (Nairobi City County, Kiambu County, Kakamega County revenue-allocation/appropriation Acts)
states.refresh_trigger: Replace this closure if Parliament enacts a uniform national ward-development-fund law (such as a future enactment of the County Wards (Equitable Development) Bill) that establishes one comparable ward-level allocation formula, or if every one of the 47 counties independently adopts a directly comparable, officially published ward-fund allocation series sharing a common definition, unit and fiscal period that could be assembled into one governed 1,450-ward series without fabricating or estimating any county's figure.
states.reason: Kenya's only nationally uniform constituency/ward-adjacent development fund is the National Government Constituencies Development Fund (NG-CDF), established and governed by the National Government Constituencies Development Fund Act, 2015 (as amended in 2022 and 2023 following the Supreme Court's August 2022 ruling that the pre-amendment Fund was unconstitutional for intruding on devolved county functions). The Act allocates and administers the Fund per constituency: Section 4 sets the national allocation formula against the 290 constituencies, and Part VI establishes one National Government Constituency Development Fund Committee per constituency to manage it. There is no ward-level NG-CDF allocation, disbursement or committee. Separately, a number of county governments have created their own 'Ward Development Fund' or 'Ward Fund' programmes through individual County Assembly Appropriation/Revenue Allocation Acts — for example Nairobi City County (increased from KES 1.4 billion to KES 2 billion across its 85 wards for FY2023/24), Kiambu County (a KES 600 million Ward Fund Bill signed into law across its 60 wards), and Kakamega County (KES 1.2 billion, about KES 20 million per ward, across its 60 wards) — with several other counties (including Embu, Nandi, Kisumu, Machakos, Murang'a, Meru, Laikipia and Nakuru) reported to have created or be creating comparable schemes. These are distinct county-specific administrative programmes created under different County Assembly Acts, with different total amounts, different per-ward formulas, different fiscal years and different governance rules; they are not present in all 47 counties and are not consolidated into one comparable national table. A national bill that would create one uniform statutory ward development fund — the County Wards (Equitable Development) Bill (most recently tabled in 2024, with an earlier 2018 version) — remains before Parliament and has not been enacted as at this review. Because no single official, uniform, nationally comparable ward-level development-fund programme currently exists across all 1,450 statistical wards, the Atlas does not construct one governed indicator value per ward. Dividing NG-CDF constituency allocations by ward count, treating an individual county's Ward Fund programme as if it were a national series, silently leaving the slot blank, or fabricating a value for counties that have not published one would each violate the cascade contract's prohibited shortcuts (never divide a parent total by arbitrary shares merely to fill child slots; never manufacture a value where none exists). The slot is therefore closed as not applicable rather than approximated, and will be revisited only if the underlying legal/programme landscape changes as described in the refresh trigger.

states.source: Ministry of Health — Kenya Master Health Facility Registry (KMHFR)
states.reason: The Atlas attempted to resolve this indicator at ward level via spatial_derivation: a point-in-polygon count of geocoded, operational KMHFR facilities against the Atlas's own canonical 1,450-ward polygon layer (data/geography/geometry/wards.geojson), divided by a ward population denominator. Both the public KMHFR facility portal and its documented GIS/API host were unreachable from the build environment on repeated attempts on 2026-09-08 (DNS resolved; every TCP connection over HTTP and HTTPS timed out or was refused), while the Ministry's own health.go.ke apex domain was reachable at the same time, showing this is a targeted access failure rather than a general outage. A systematic search for a genuine alternative official geocoded facility list found none that qualifies: the only official KMHFR-derived extract available for download (HDX "Kenya - Health facilities in Kenya", 2017) has no latitude/longitude field at all and is a 2017 snapshot of 8,932 facilities that predates and does not reconcile to the 2023 Kenya Health Facility Census total (14,883 facilities) already anchoring this indicator at county level; the only current, geocoded facility datasets found (healthsites.io's "Kenya Healthsites" export and the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team's "Health Facilities of Kenya" export) are both built from OpenStreetMap volunteer mapping rather than an official government registry and both self-disclose incomplete, geographically uneven coverage, so neither can support a Class C spatially-derived observation under the Atlas data-quality framework, which requires a documented official input for that class. Independently, the ward population denominator required for a facilities-per-10,000-residents rate does not yet exist in the canonical registry (IND-POPULATION currently resolves only to country and county level). A facility count is not relabelled as a population density, and no county or constituency value is inherited downward to any ward.
states.refresh_trigger: Replace this closure when KMHFR (or another authoritative Ministry of Health facility registry) becomes reachable with geocoordinates, or another genuine official geocoded national facility list is published, AND an official ward-level (or higher-resolution, deterministically aggregable) population denominator compatible with the facility reference period is available — enabling a real point-in-polygon spatial_derivation against data/geography/geometry/wards.geojson.

Re-open this closure if IEBC (or another primary official statistical authority) publishes a single already-aggregated, citable ward-level turnout table (analogous to the Gazette Notice No. 7290 First Schedule already used for IND-REGISTERED-VOTERS), or if a dedicated ward-level extraction programme is undertaken that mirrors the P23 Form34B source-verification pipeline (per-document image review, field-level verification, promotion-eligibility gating) applied to either Form 34A polling-station presidential results re-summed to ward boundaries, or Form 36B ward-level MCA tally sheets, and produces source-verified per-ward registered-voter, valid-vote and rejected-ballot triples.
states.reason: Voter turnout in prior general elections (IND-TURNOUT-HISTORY) is only defensible when computed from a registered-voter denominator and a valid-plus-rejected-vote numerator for the same geography and election. No official body publishes a single already-aggregated, citable ward-level turnout table. The IEBC Result Forms Portal (forms.iebc.or.ke) exposes only individual scanned per-polling-station and per-tallying-centre result form images, not a pre-aggregated ward statistic. IEBC's published registered-voters-per-ward table (rov_per_caw.pdf) supplies only the electorate denominator, not votes cast. IEBC's 2022 Post-Election Evaluation Report is a national narrative/summary document with no ward-by-ward turnout table. Third-party sites that present ward-level figures (e.g. KenyaTally, TransTally) re-publish the same underlying IEBC portal form images rather than an independent official aggregate, and are not a primary statistical authority under this Atlas's source-priority rules. The two forms that could in principle support ward turnout are: (a) Form 34A, the polling-station presidential result, which would need to be re-summed to ward boundaries across roughly 46,000 polling stations nationwide -- a substantially larger extraction task than the Form 34B constituency pipeline already built in P23; and (b) Form 36B, the ward-level MCA tally sheet, which is the direct ward analogue of Form 34B but exists only as 1,450 individual scanned per-ward documents with no established, source-verified extraction pipeline in this repository. Building and running that pipeline is a dedicated future programme of the same class as the multi-week P23 Form34B effort, at up to five times the geographic unit count, and is out of scope for a single session. The Atlas does not copy constituency-level turnout down to wards (explicitly prohibited by the Local Indicator Cascade Contract), does not estimate ward turnout from registered-voter shares or any other proxy, and does not promote unverified OCR candidates. All 1,450 statistical ward slots for IND-TURNOUT-HISTORY are therefore closed as governed official_unavailable rather than filled with a fabricated, inherited or unverified number.
